the-fight-for-a-homeowners-meeting.text: The fight for a homeowners' meeting

pageProps.body:
Resettlement & Owners

Parent: 🔥 Hong Kong Fire 2025

What happens to the ~2,000 flats and their owners after the fire is a story of its own: a government buyback of the seven ruined blocks, a long fight by owners for a statutory meeting with the government-appointed administrator, and the scramble for somewhere to live. This page gathers that thread. For the people living through it, see the displaced-resident profiles on People; for the dated sequence, Timeline.

The buyback scheme

  • The plan (21 Feb 2026). The government offered to buy back flats in the seven fire-damaged blocks at HK$8,000/sq ft (without land premium) or HK$10,500/sq ft (with), with flat-for-flat exchanges available from 10 Home Ownership Scheme / Housing Society projects. Wang Chi House — the one block largely spared — was initially excluded. Redevelopment was ruled out, the government citing a 9–10-year timeline (SCMP).
  • The money (25 Feb 2026 Budget). HK$4b public funds + HK$2.8b from the Support Fund = HK$6.8b earmarked. An early survey found 74% would consider acquisition and 9% insisted on redevelopment only.
  • Offer letters (14 May 2026) went out at the HK$8,000–10,500/sq ft terms, with a 75% acceptance threshold and a flat-selection deadline of 30 June.
  • Hop On (the administrator) began refunding ~HK$127m of the renovation fund that had financed the deadly works.

Rehousing options

Transitional and permanent rehousing was spread across several estates and years: Shing Chi Court (Kowloon Bay, from Sep 2026); Kam Tin Wui Hei Court (late Aug 2027); and new Tai Po developments at Chung Nga Road West (2029) and Kwong Fuk Park (2033). Many displaced residents are elderly and wanted to stay in Tai Po; the long timelines pushed some to accept flats in other districts (see the profiles on People).

Uptake — and the 17 holdouts

  • Over 85% of fire-hit-block owners had accepted by the 30 June flat-selection deadline.
  • By the 31 August deadline, 99.1% (1,967 of 1,984) had accepted — leaving 17 holdouts, who face compulsory acquisition, with compensation likely pegged to the lower post-fire value and enabling legislation flagged for 2027.
  • Wang Chi House (the spared block) was brought in with a separate ~HK$1b offer (extended in June): by 21 August, 91.5% of its owners had accepted and 67.7% had signed sale-and-purchase agreements, against a 15 October signing deadline (the final tally is not yet reported).

The fight for a homeowners' meeting

After the fire, the government installed Hop On Management (a Chinachem subsidiary) as the estate's administrator. Owners spent months trying to force a statutory general meeting to get answers on funds, insurance and their future housing — and were repeatedly blocked.

  • Online petition → forgery referral (5–10 Apr 2026). Owners gathered a petition (428 valid signatures, above the 5% Building Management Ordinance threshold of ~100 of 1,984 units) to compel a general meeting. Hop On rejected it on 5 April; on 10 April the Home Affairs Department referred the petition to law enforcement, alleging it "lacked authentication mechanisms and may involve people impersonating owners and forging signatures" (HKFP).
  • Owners regroup (29 Apr 2026). Undeterred, owners delivered 247 handwritten signatures (~12% of households). Under the BMO this obliged Hop On to issue a meeting notice within 14 days (by 14 May) and hold the meeting within 45 days (HKFP).
  • The administrator stalls (14–20 May 2026). On the notice deadline, Hop On instead asked the Lands Tribunal to extend the statutory timeframe, citing signature verification and venue logistics, and held online-only "information sessions" (from 20 May) with no voting and reported registration glitches (HKFP).
  • Tribunal rejects the delay (1–2 Jun 2026). Lands Tribunal Judge Gary Lam denied the postponement: there was no jurisdiction under the BMO to vary the timeframe, and delay would infringe owners' right to a meeting — Hop On already held contact details for 1,601 of 1,984 owners, so the difficulty was "not insurmountable" (HKFP).
  • Government backs the administrator (9 Jun 2026). CE John Lee defended Hop On over the delay, drawing criticism that officials were shielding the administrator rather than enforcing the meeting owners had demanded since March (HKFP).
  • First statutory meeting (19 Jul 2026). The meeting finally convened across four venues. Owners rejected Hop On's audit report but backed holding a second meeting within two months.

Belongings retrieval (20 Apr – 4 May 2026)

Announced by Deputy Chief Secretary Warner Cheuk (卓永興) on 27 March, retrieval ran in 3-hour slots, stairs only, max four people per flat, with 1,000 personnel deployed. On day one (Wang Sun House, 1F–10F), 264 of 267 registered residents attended; average stay 1h 44min; one resident in his 70s was hospitalised with breathing difficulty and discharged the same day; of 11 missing-item reports, 4 were recovered, 4 judged destroyed, and 3 placed under police investigation (HKFP, The Witness).

Relief payments

Separate from the buyback, a government-led Wang Fuk Court Assistance Fund (~HK$2.3b: ~HK$2b donations + HK$300m government seed) made emergency disbursements: HK$200,000 condolence and HK$50,000 funeral per fatality, and HK$50,000 living allowance per affected household (announced by Secretary for Home and Youth Affairs Alice Mak). For the corporate and philanthropic donation roster, see Donations and Aid on Activism.

See also

  • People — displaced-resident profiles (Pearl Chow, Kit Chan, Isaac Tam and others).
  • Activism — the homeowners'-meeting fight as civic action, and the donation roster.
  • Timeline — the dated sequence.

noteIndex.title: SHKO(Save Hong Kong Online)
noteIndex.body:
[![Great Extinction](/assets/extinctions.jpeg)](/notes/wx39zljncctue32jn06u29u/) 
> (_Courtesy: [Hong Kong Freepress](https://hongkongfp.com/2021/11/28/explainer-over-50-groups-gone-in-11-months-how-hong-kongs-pro-democracy-forces-crumbled/), 2021_) 

SHKO (Save Hong Kong Online) is a community-driven project dedicated to preserving the rapidly disappearing websites and online resources of Hong Kong’s civil society and independent media since 2019. In response to the sweeping shutdowns caused by political changes in Hong Kong, we aim to safeguard digital heritage before it vanishes. This project is anonymous, open source, and supported by a global network of contributors.

While most sites in our archive were forced offline due to Hong Kong’s political deterioration, it’s important to note that [[RFA Cantonese|sites.rfa_cantonese]] is the only site here closed not because of Hong Kong’s situation, but due to internal political decisions in the United States.

Explore our full list of preserved sites and archives on the [Collections page](/notes/wx39zljncctue32jn06u29u/).

Recent work: documenting the [[Hong Kong Fire 2025|hong-kong-fire-2025]] tragedy at Wang Fuk Court (168 dead, ongoing probes into flammable mesh/foam, bid-rigging, and a judge-led review), including activism, timeline, and investigation subpages; and the [[⚖️ Jimmy Lai case|faces-of-the-crackdown.jimmy-lai]] — Apple Daily founder sentenced to 20 years under the National Security Law (Feb 2026), with coverage of press freedom impact and international response; and [[🎵 Glory to Hong Kong|glory-to-hong-kong]] — the 2019 protest anthem and the 2024 court order that made it the first song banned in Hong Kong since the 1997 handover; and [[📕 Book Censorship under the NSL|book-censorship]] — how Hong Kong criminalised the printed word, from the banned Sheep Village children's-book trilogy (whose speech-therapist authors were jailed for sedition) and purged public libraries to the 2026 bookshop raids; and [[🗽 Statues & Monuments|statues]] — how Hong Kong's public monuments to Tiananmen and the 2019 protests (the Pillar of Shame, the Goddess of Democracy, Lady Liberty) were removed, seized as police evidence, and driven into exile abroad; and [[⚖️ The Hong Kong 47|hong-kong-47]] — the largest National Security Law case, in which 45 pro-democracy figures were jailed for up to 10 years over a 2020 opposition primary election; and [[🕯️ Tiananmen Vigil|tiananmen-vigil]] — the thirty-year Victoria Park candlelight vigil for the 1989 crackdown, the largest June 4th commemoration on Chinese soil, now banned and its organisers jailed; and [[✊ Faces of the Crackdown|faces-of-the-crackdown]] — a human index to the publishers, students, unionists and clergy jailed, exiled or tried under the National Security Law; and [[🎬 Films & Documentaries|films]] — the protest movement on film, a decade of documentaries and features (Ten Years, Revolution of Our Times, the Joshua Wong doc) now largely banned or unshowable in Hong Kong, gathered with their trailers; and [[📰 Press Freedom under Siege|press-freedom]] — how one of Asia's freest presses was dismantled in five years, from the raids that closed Apple Daily and Stand News to the revived sedition law now reaching lone online reporters.

## Goals
- To preserve as much information as possible before its disappearance during Hong Kong's great transition
- To illustrate a viable method that everyone can use to help preserve online heritage with no pains
- To demonstrate global collaborations to save local digital heritages with best practices

## Quick Facts

We are working on over dozens of [[websites or online causes | sites]] in Hong Kong in the past two decades which has been forced to shutdown or at the brink of disappearing. We'd welcome anyone help [[contribute | participation]] to the content and/or [[sponsor | sponsorship]] our program to sustain it together. 

Examples:
- [[sites.appledaily]] (Extincted)
- [[sites.inmediahk]] (In Danger)
